title: Market data replay for backtesting: a full day of US equities from QuestDB
summary: A full trading day of US equities, 354 million top-of-book events, streamed back from QuestDB as Arrow. In strict time order the client peaks at 194 MiB; parallel connections reach 14 Gb/s, using more memory as more results arrive at once. Code, commands and hardware included so you can rerun it.
body_markdown:
QuestDB is the open-source time-series database for demanding workloads—from trading floors to mission control. It delivers ultra-low latency, high ingestion throughput, and a multi-tier storage engine. Native support for Parquet and SQL keeps your data portable, AI-ready—no vendor lock-in.


---


A backtest only gives an honest answer if the past arrives in the order it happened, every quote and trade fed to the same code that will later run live. That makes replay the job a tick store is judged on.


kdb+ built much of its reputation on that job, and its license includes a DeWitt clause, so you can't publish your own kdb+ benchmarks.


What we can show you is how fast QuestDB does it. Below is a full day of every US equity, replayed out of QuestDB as fast as it goes, with the code, the commands and the hardware, so you can rerun it on your own machines and against whatever you run today.


The data comes from Databento's` EQUS.MINI` , loaded as in our[previous post](https://questdb.com/blog/ingest-databento-market-data-questdb/) : 354 million top-of-book events and 7.5 million trades, 57.6 GB once decoded into Arrow.


- **Strict order:** about two minutes for the whole day, at 3.5 to 3.8 Gb/s
- **Eight connections per table:** 32.5 seconds, at 14.2 Gb/s
- **Client memory:** 194 MiB at peak, about half of it the idle Python process
- **One symbol, NVDA:** 5.6 to 6.0 seconds end to end, filter included


Replaying one full trading day. Grey bars ran on the database host, with no network.

of Arrow in one full replay

The replay works the same on QuestDB open source and QuestDB Enterprise, and the code is in our[blog-examples repository](https://github.com/questdb/blog-examples/tree/main/2026-11-market-data-replay) .


---


## One trading day of US equities top of book, in one table


Databento's` EQUS.MINI` blends feeds from US exchanges and alternative trading systems into one composite best bid and offer per stock, plus the trades. We loaded two of its schemas for October 27th, 2026:` mbp-1` , every change to the top of book, into` equs_all_orderbook` , and` trades` into` equs_all_trades` .` mbp-1` also carries the trade events, so the order book table on its own is one complete, ordered stream of quotes and trades.


Table Rows Symbols On disk


` equs_all_orderbook` 353,657,441 12,684 79.2 GB


` equs_all_trades` 7,544,547 9,802 0.6 GB


The session runs from 04:00 to 20:00 New York time, but the day isn't even. Regular hours, 09:30 to 16:00, hold 98% of the book events:


Top-of-book events per 5 minutes, Databento EQUS.MINI, Tuesday 2026-10-27, every US equity


98%


of events in regular hours


206,101


events in the busiest second


2.5M


events in the last minute before the close


The busiest second of the day carried 206,101 book events, and the last minute before the close carried 2.5 million. Those are the moments a backtest cares most about, and the ones a sampled or bar-based dataset smooths away.


Both tables come from the[Databento connector](https://questdb.com/docs/connect/connectors/databento/) in Historical mode, which is a QuestDB Enterprise feature. The[previous post](https://questdb.com/blog/ingest-databento-market-data-questdb/) covers the connector and the table layout, and the example repository has a` backfill_day.py` script that loads a day for NVDA and AAPL, or every symbol with` --all-symbols` . On QuestDB open source, load the data with the[Databento Python guide](https://questdb.com/docs/integrations/other/databento/) instead, and the replay below works unchanged.


Every row is wide: 18 columns, four of them arrays.


equs_all_orderbook


```text
CREATE TABLE equs_all_orderbook (       dataset SYMBOL,                -- EQUS.MINI       symbol SYMBOL CAPACITY 16384,  -- NVDA, AAPL, ... 12,684 of them       publisher_id INT,              -- venue the record came from       instrument_id LONG,       ts_event TIMESTAMP_NS,         -- when the venue saw the event       price DOUBLE,       size LONG,       action SYMBOL,                 -- A add, C cancel, T trade, ...       side SYMBOL,                   -- B bid, A ask, N none       flags SHORT,       depth SHORT,       ts_recv TIMESTAMP_NS,          -- when Databento received it       ts_in_delta LONG,       sequence LONG,       bids DOUBLE[][],               -- [[prices], [sizes]], best level first       asks DOUBLE[][],       bid_ct DOUBLE[],               -- orders at each bid level       ask_ct DOUBLE[]   ) TIMESTAMP(ts_recv) PARTITION BY DAY WAL;
```


This is what the replay streams back. The first NVDA events after the 09:30 open, in the Web Console, with 8 of those 18 columns:


NVDA at the open


```text
SELECT ts_recv, symbol, action, side, price, size, bids, asks   FROM equs_all_orderbook   WHERE symbol = 'NVDA'     AND ts_recv IN '2026-10-27T13:30:00Z;1s'   LIMIT 8;
```


The first NVDA book events after the open, with nanosecond timestamps


Each row is one event, and` bids` and` asks` hold the top of the book right after it:` \[\[217.63\], \[20.0\]\]` is 20 shares bid at 217.63. Each array has one level because` mbp-1` is top of book only. A deeper schema such as` mbp-10` uses the same columns with more levels, and wider rows.


---


## How the replay streams from QuestDB: Arrow batches over QWP


The replay script,` replay.py` , uses the[QuestDB Python client](https://questdb.com/docs/connect/clients/python/#querying) , which reads over[QWP](https://questdb.com/blog/questdb-qwp-binary-wire-protocol/) , QuestDB's binary protocol over WebSocket. Results come back as a stream of[Apache Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org/) record batches of up to 16,384 rows each, and the loop at the heart of the script hands each one to the consumer as it arrives:


replay.py, reading one query


```text
with reader.query(sql, reset_symbol_dict=False) as result:       for batch in result.iter_arrow():           timestamps = to_ns(batch.column("ts_recv"))           out_of_order += np.count_nonzero(np.diff(timestamps) < 0)           publish(table, batch)
```


` publish()` is where your consumer goes: a strategy, a Kafka producer, an order book rebuild. In the runs below it's empty, so they measure reading. Whatever you put there sets the pace, and a slow consumer slows its connection down through QWP's flow control rather than piling batches up in memory. Once` publish()` returns, the batch is released, which is why the client's memory depends on how many connections are open, not on how many rows a query returns. The` out_of_order` counter checks the ordering on every batch, and it was zero in every run.


### Why the day is split into a few queries


In principle the whole day is one query:` SELECT * FROM equs_all_orderbook` , streamed in timestamp order. In practice every query has to finish within the server's` query.timeout` , 60 seconds by default, and a strict replay of the book takes two minutes or more. So the script cuts each table into consecutive time ranges with about the same number of rows, using per-minute counts from QuestDB:


Rows per minute, used to plan the time ranges


```text
SELECT ts_recv minute, count() rows   FROM equs_all_orderbook   SAMPLE BY 1m;
```


Each connection gets one range, split further only so that no single query exceeds 100 million rows. In strict order the book becomes four queries of about 88 million rows, read one after another on the same connection. The split has no other purpose, and the per-query overhead is negligible.


Info


As of the writing of this post, a per-query timeout for QWP is in progress (see[questdb/questdb#7768](https://github.com/questdb/questdb/pull/7768) ). Once it ships in the server and the Python client, a strict replay won't need splitting at all.


---


## Strict-order replay: 354 million book events at up to 3.8 Gb/s


By default the example script opens one QuestDB connection per table and sends its queries one after another. QuestDB returns each query's rows in` ts_recv` order, so the table arrives in strict order:


```text
export QDB_CLIENT_CONF='wss::addr=<server>:9000;token=<token>;'   python3 replay.py equs_all_orderbook equs_all_trades
```


```text
equs_all_orderbook: 353,657,441 rows, 0 out of order, 129.0s, 2,742,501 rows/s, 441.6 MB/s   equs_all_trades: 7,544,547 rows, 0 out of order, 1.1s, 6,575,707 rows/s, 534.3 MB/s   Replayed 361,201,988 rows over 2 connection(s) in 129.0s (2,801,006 rows/s)
```


Across runs on different days, the order book took between 119.2 and 130.4 seconds, which is 3.5 to 3.8 Gb/s. The trades table finishes in about a second on its own connection while the book carries on.


On the server this used 1.2 of its 32 cores, almost all of it in one network thread. With one connection per table, strict order can't use more than that, and that one thread is the limit. Running the client on the database host doesn't lift it either: strict order took 117.6 to 129.9 seconds there.


### Why Gb/s and not rows per second


These rows are wide, about 160 bytes each once decoded into Arrow. The same machinery moves a narrow five-column trades table at[220 million rows a second](https://questdb.com/blog/streaming-500-million-rows-into-apache-arrow/) . Rows per second mostly measures how wide the rows are. Gigabits per second, counted as the decoded Arrow bytes handed to the consumer, is the figure that carries over to your own schema, so it's the one we quote throughout.


---


## Client memory stays flat while 57.6 GB streams through


The replay never holds the day, so the client's memory tracks the number of open connections, not the amount of data:


Run Arrow streamed Peak client memory (RSS)


Strict order, 2 connections About 57.6 GB 194 MiB


Parallel, 10 connections About 57.6 GB 535 MiB


A Python process with the client libraries loaded sits at about 100 MiB before it receives anything, so strict order added under 100 MiB on top of that while reading the whole day. A table ten times larger should need the same.


On the server, used memory stayed between 1.5 and 1.8 GB for the whole run, and the page cache sat flat at 78.7 GB because the day was already in it.


---


## Parallel replay: 14.2 Gb/s, until the network runs out


Not every replay needs global order. Fitting a model per time window, checking features range by range, or warming a cache over a whole day only need each range in order internally. For those, the example script's` --connections` option opens that many QuestDB connections per table and gives each one an equal share of the day to query. QuestDB serves the queries side by side:


```text
python3 replay.py equs_all_orderbook equs_all_trades --connections 8
```


```text
equs_all_orderbook: 353,657,441 rows, 0 out of order, 32.5s, 10,882,357 rows/s, 1,752.3 MB/s   equs_all_trades: 7,544,547 rows, 0 out of order, 1.1s, 6,975,148 rows/s, 566.7 MB/s   Replayed 361,201,988 rows over 10 connection(s) in 32.5s (11,114,510 rows/s)
```


Both tables in 32.5 seconds, about 11 million rows a second and 14.2 Gb/s of decoded Arrow. Rows are in order within each connection's share, which is what the zero counts, and not across shares. We kept it that way on purpose: putting the shares back in order would mean buffering them, and the point of this mode is speed.


The limit here is the network. Arrow takes more room in memory than on the wire, so the 14.2 Gb/s the client decoded crossed the network as 12.2 Gb/s on average, peaking at 12.5. That's the ceiling: the server is rated at 12.5 Gbps, and the client at up to 12.5 Gbps as a burst above a lower baseline. QuestDB used 8.8 of its 32 cores to get there.


### Removing the network: 27 Gb/s on the database host


To see what's behind that ceiling, we ran the client on the server itself, connecting to` localhost` and pinned with` taskset` to cores away from QuestDB's threads:


Run, connections per table Time Rows/s Decoded throughput


Over the network, 8 32.5 s 11.11M 14.2 Gb/s


On the server, 8 18.7 s 19.36M 24.6 Gb/s


On the server, 16 17.0 s 21.19M 27.1 Gb/s


With the same eight connections, taking the network away made the replay 74% faster. Doubling to 16 added about 10% more, at which point one Python process serves every connection and the client shares the server's CPUs with TLS and loopback copies. These are ceilings, not deployment figures, since nobody runs a backtest on the database host. They show how much room QuestDB has before it becomes the limit.


---


## Replaying one symbol in order: NVDA end to end


A backtest on a single stock doesn't need the other 12,683 symbols. The script's` --symbol` option adds` symbol = 'NVDA'` to every query's filter, and QuestDB still returns the rows in timestamp order:


```text
python3 replay.py equs_all_orderbook equs_all_trades --symbol NVDA
```


```text
equs_all_orderbook: 1,382,513 rows, 0 out of order, 6.0s, 229,980 rows/s, 36.8 MB/s   equs_all_trades: 29,879 rows, 0 out of order, 0.1s, 268,773 rows/s, 21.5 MB/s   Replayed 1,412,392 rows over 2 connection(s) in 6.0s (234,950 rows/s)
```


Those 5.6 to 6.0 seconds across runs are end to end: QuestDB finds NVDA's rows, 0.4% of the day's 354 million, and streams them as it finds them, while the client receives and checks every batch. Those rows are scattered across the whole day's files, and reading them from all over the day is what takes the time. With` --connections 8` , the script splits NVDA's rows equally across eight connections, and they arrive in 0.9 seconds, in order within each connection's share.


---


## Where these replay numbers stop: page cache, consumers and book depth


Every figure above comes from the same setup, and a few things would change them:


- **The day was in memory.** The server had 78.7 GB of page cache holding the whole day, so no run read from disk. A server that can't cache the day reads part of it from storage, and these numbers don't apply.
- **` publish()` was empty.** A consumer that does per-row work in Python, or buffers the day, will be slower and use more memory. The replay will wait for it.
- **Top of book only.** One level per side. A deeper book such as` mbp-10` makes every row bigger, so Gb/s should stay about the same while fewer rows arrive each second.
- **Tables are independent.** With two tables in strict order, each arrives in order on its own. Because` mbp-1` already includes trades, the order book table is the single merged stream here. For other datasets, a merge of two streams on the timestamp belongs in the consumer.


Your numbers will differ with hardware, network and schema, which is why everything is published.


---


## Run the replay on your own hardware


The runs above used an EC2 m7a.8xlarge for QuestDB and an m7a.2xlarge client in the same availability zone. To run the replay on your own hardware, the[example repository](https://github.com/questdb/blog-examples/tree/main/2026-11-market-data-replay) has the script and every command, from loading the day to the one-symbol runs. It works with QuestDB open source 10.0 or later and QuestDB Enterprise 4.0 or later. Loading the data through the Databento connector needs QuestDB Enterprise; on open source, load it with the[Databento Python guide](https://questdb.com/docs/integrations/other/databento/) .


If you have a kdb+ estate, the comparison we can't publish is one you can run yourself: the same day, the same consumer, your tickerplant log or HDB on one side and this script on the other. The[QuestDB vs kdb+ page](https://questdb.com/compare/questdb-vs-kdb/) covers the rest of the architecture. Getting the data out fast is also what feeds[transaction cost analysis in Polars](https://questdb.com/blog/transaction-cost-analysis-questdb-polars/) , and the[Arrow egress benchmark](https://questdb.com/blog/streaming-500-million-rows-into-apache-arrow/) compares the same read path with ClickHouse and TimescaleDB. If you rerun this, tell us what you measured on the[community forum](https://community.questdb.com/) .
